short: Constantine's vast basilica on the Vatican Hill, raised over a site believed to hold Saint Peter's grave.
full:
Constantine ordered a huge basilica built on the Vatican Hill, on the far bank of the Tiber from the city centre, over a modest shrine that Roman Christians had long identified as the burial site of Saint Peter. Building began around 319 CE and the church was substantially complete by 333, though decoration continued for years afterward, an unusually fast pace achieved partly by levelling part of an existing pagan cemetery on the site and building the nave's foundations directly over sealed tombs rather than clearing them.

The finished basilica had five aisles under a timber roof, a nave over 90 metres long leading to an apse and transept marking the supposed grave site, and an open colonnaded forecourt, or atrium, before its entrance. It became the site of imperial coronations and papal ceremony for over a thousand years. By the fifteenth century the structure was unstable, and it was demolished in stages from 1506 to make way for the present St Peter's Basilica, completed in the seventeenth century.
